opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest value shows up in large, messy codebases where the hard part isn't writing code, it's understanding what's already there. If you're an engineer at a big company, a huge fraction of your time goes into figuring out how some system works, who touched it last, why a certain decision was made, and what will break if you change it. That context-gathering is slow and tedious, and it's exactly the kind of work an agent that can go off, read through hundreds of files, trace dependencies, and come back with a synthesized answer is really well suited for.

So the way we think about it is less "autocomplete on steroids" and more like a very fast, very thorough colleague who has read the whole codebase. You ask a question like, "How does authentication flow through our services?" or "Why is this test flaky?" and instead of you spending an afternoon spelunking, the agent spends a few minutes doing that research and gives you a grounded answer with references back to the actual code.

The second place it helps a lot is onboarding. New engineers on a team often take weeks or months before they're really productive, mostly because of missing context. If you can compress that ramp-up period, that's enormously valuable for the organization.

And then once you have that deep understanding, the actual code generation gets much better too, because the changes are informed by how the system really works rather than by a narrow window of the file you happen to have open. In our view, understanding comes first, and good code follows from it.

r001.rationale: The response describes deep research as useful for understanding large codebases, but does not say quick questions about a known file location are a poor fit.

r002.rationale: It mentions asking why a test is flaky, but does not clearly identify diagnosing a symptom when the code location is unknown as a particularly valuable use.

r003.rationale: The response discusses gathering context from the codebase and does not state that diagnostic knowledge may reside outside it.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe individually test-passing changes interacting to cause a performance regression.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that the biggest value isn't in writing code at all. It's in the time before you write code.

If you look at how a senior engineer actually spends a week on a large, mature codebase, maybe twenty percent of it is typing. The rest is figuring out what's going on. Why does this service behave this way? Which of the fourteen places this config gets read is the one that matters? Who changed this, when, and what were they trying to do? That's the work that's painful, and it's the work that doesn't fit in a single autocomplete or a single chat window, because the answer is spread across hundreds of files, a few years of git history, some design docs, and a Slack thread nobody can find anymore.

So the "deep research" framing is deliberate. We wanted an agent that goes and does that investigation for you. It reads the code, follows the call graph, reads the history, runs things if it needs to, and comes back with a grounded answer with citations into the actual repo. Not "here's a plausible function," but "here's how this system really works, here are the three places you'd need to touch, and here's the risk in each one."

Where that lands hardest is a few places. One is onboarding. A new engineer joining a team with a million-line codebase normally takes months to become productive. If you can compress the "how does this all fit together" phase from months to days, that's enormous. Two is the large refactor or migration, where the hard part is scoping it correctly, not executing it. And three is incident response and debugging, where you're under pressure and need to go from "something's wrong" to "here's the root cause" quickly, and you don't have time to grep around for an hour.

The way I'd put it is: the assistants we've had so far make the fast part of engineering faster. We think the real leverage is making the slow part fast. Once the understanding is right, the code is actually the easy bit, and the agent can do that too. But if you skip the understanding, you just generate wrong code faster, and anyone who's worked on real systems knows that's worse than nothing.

r001.rationale: The response says deep research helps when answers are spread across many files and other sources, but it does not identify quick questions about a known file location as a poor fit.

r002.rationale: It describes incident response as moving from “something's wrong” to the root cause quickly under pressure, which communicates value in diagnosing a problem without an initial location to inspect.

r003.rationale: It says relevant answers may be spread across code, git history, design docs, and a hard-to-find Slack thread, clearly placing needed knowledge outside the codebase.

r004.rationale: The response does not describe individually passing code changes interacting to cause a performance regression.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest value is in tasks where the bottleneck is figuring out what to do, rather than typing the code. You come into an unfamiliar codebase, there’s a bug that crosses a few different systems, or you want to make a change and you don’t know what it’s going to break. A lot of the work is building enough context to make a good decision.

That’s where a deep research-style assistant can be useful: tracing how things fit together, exploring possible explanations, running tests, and coming back with a change and evidence that it works. The engineer can focus on the requirements and the tradeoffs instead of personally following every lead.

The interesting question is how much of that investigation you can delegate reliably. If you have to supervise every step, you haven’t saved very much. If you can hand it a well-defined problem and come back to something you can meaningfully review, that’s a much bigger shift.

r001.rationale: The response describes complex investigations as valuable but does not identify quick questions about a known file location as a poor fit.

r002.rationale: It mentions tracing bugs across systems, but does not clearly say the assistant is especially useful when diagnosing a symptom without knowing where to look in the code.

r003.rationale: The response discusses building context in an unfamiliar codebase but does not state that relevant diagnostic knowledge may be outside the codebase.

r004.rationale: It mentions running tests, but not individually passing changes interacting to cause a performance regression.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it provides the most value when you know what you want to accomplish, but you don’t yet know where in the codebase to make the change or what the right approach is. There’s a lot of engineering work between getting a task and writing the first line of code: understanding the system, tracing dependencies, figuring out what’s already been tried, and deciding how you’re going to test it.

That’s where a deep research-style assistant can be useful. You can give it an objective, and it can spend time investigating the codebase, trying an approach, running tests, and revising based on what it finds. The valuable output is a change that’s grounded in how your system actually works, with enough evidence that you can review it and trust it.

So I’d expect the biggest benefit on tasks that take an engineer hours or days of investigation, especially in an unfamiliar part of a large codebase. Typing the code is often a relatively small part of that work.

r001.rationale: It emphasizes substantial investigation as valuable but does not identify quick questions about a known file location as a poor fit.

r002.rationale: It describes uncertainty about where to make a change, but does not specifically identify diagnosing a symptom without knowing where to look as a particularly valuable use.

r003.rationale: It discusses investigating the codebase and its dependencies, but does not state that diagnostic knowledge may reside outside the codebase.

r004.rationale: It mentions testing and revising, but does not explain that individually passing code changes can interact and cause a performance regression.
